I enjoy learning new things, exploring creative ideas, and working with others to develop solutions to real-world challenges. I'm excited to collaborate, share ideas, and contribute my skills to this project.
summary:
The Last Lap is a free, bilingual (English/Spanish) website that teaches how real space missions are designed, by letting you run one. It needs no installation and works on phones, tablets and computers.
The problem: NASA's mission design resources (mission segments, Concept Maturity Levels, trade studies, GMAT trajectories) are powerful but written for professionals, so most students never learn why a rocket launches on a certain day or how engineers balance money, risk and science.
Our solution follows a hypothetical mission that uses the Moon as a gravity slingshot to reach Mars. Animations and a 3D mission viewer explain orbits, the opposition of Mars, the slingshot effect and aerobraking. In the game you are the mission director: you choose a science goal, which decides the instrument and ideal landing site, then a rocket, crew and supplies within a budget, moving through CML 1-4. Every chapter is tagged with its mission segment, situations change each game, and skill mini-games test your decisions. At the end you see real missions similar to yours (Perseverance, InSight, MAVEN...). A 45-minute lesson plan helps teachers use it in class.
We used 8 NASA resources and 1 CSA resource, each cited on the site with the data we took from it. Built with the help of Claude (Anthropic). NASA does not endorse this project.
details:
What it does and how it works

The Last Lap is a free, bilingual (English/Spanish) website that teaches how real space missions are designed by letting you run one. It follows a hypothetical mission that uses the Moon as a gravity slingshot on the way to Mars, and it has three parts:

Learn: animated sections explain orbits, the opposition of Mars, the slingshot effect, aerobraking, Mars' lost magnetic field and communication delays. A section explains the 4 mission segments (launch, space, ground and user). A rotatable 3D mission viewer with a timeline shows where Earth, the Moon, Mars and the spacecraft are on each day of the trip.

Play: in the game "From launch to Mars: your decisions" you are the mission director.

Preparation: you choose a science goal (water, ancient life, climate or quakes). It decides the only instrument that fits and the ideal landing site. Then you choose a rocket, crew, supplies and tools within a budget, moving through Concept Maturity Levels 1–4.

The trip: each chapter is tagged with its mission segment, and every decision changes money, fuel, supplies, crew health and the ship's condition.

Variety: situations change every game (solar storms, fuel leaks, space debris, dust storms…). Skill mini-games (slingshot timing, aerobraking, antenna pointing, rewiring cables, photographing Mars from orbit) and quick science quizzes test what you learned.

The ending: you land, or photograph Mars from orbit, and see real missions similar to yours (Perseverance, Curiosity, InSight, MAVEN, Phoenix…).

Teach: an Impact section includes a ready-to-use 45-minute lesson for teachers, with questions for students.

Benefits

Free and easy to access: no sign-up and no installation; it works on phones, tablets and computers and is available in English and Spanish.

Learning by doing: it turns technical NASA resources into decisions students can understand and experience.

Real science, clearly labelled: every simplification is marked on the page, and every NASA resource is cited with the specific data we used from it.

Intended impact

We want students aged 12–18 and their teachers to understand that missions follow a real engineering process: science goal → requirements → trade-offs → design → operations. We have not yet measured learning with students. Our next step is to use the website in classrooms in our region, check with the game's quizzes which concepts are learned, and add more languages.

Tools, languages and software

Code: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks.

Graphics: SVG and the Canvas 2D API for all the illustrations, animations and the 3D viewer, drawn with code (no AI-generated images).

Browser APIs: Web Audio for sound effects, Web Speech plus voice recordings made by our team for the characters, and localStorage for saving games, medals and the chosen language.

Images: public-domain NASA photos: Apollo 17 "Blue Marble", Hubble's 2003 Mars and an LRO Moon mosaic.

Development: GitHub for version control, Vercel for hosting and Playwright for automated testing on desktop and mobile.

AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic) helped us program, translate and research NASA resources. The team defined the idea and the content and reviewed the result.

Hardware: no special hardware; we developed and tested on regular computers, phones and tablets.

Creativity

Instead of just reading about mission design, players live it: the Moon becomes a free push to Mars, each decision is a real trade-off, and the game ends by connecting your mission to real NASA missions. Each NASA resource became a game mechanic:

The 4 mission segments became chapter labels.

Concept Maturity Levels became the preparation steps.

The Mission Design Lab's trade studies became the cost/risk/benefit choices.

The telescope learning game inspired the science goal that limits which instruments fit.

Mission Viz inspired the 3D viewer.

Factors we considered

Scientific validity: real orbital mechanics (opposition, Hohmann transfer, aerobraking, light delay), with exaggerations clearly marked.

Accessibility:

Keyboard controls, support for reduced motion and touch-friendly mini-games.

Every screen fits on a phone.

English and Spanish versions.

Different players: three difficulty levels, so beginners and advanced players can both enjoy it.

Low barrier to entry: a light website that loads in any browser.

Honesty and rights: proper credits for NASA images, no NASA logos, a clear statement that NASA does not endorse the project, and transparency about using AI.
